common_name: Shanghai Green Pak Choi (Dwarf Green-Stem Bok Choy)

planting.note: Direct sow from early spring through late summer for successive crops; Shanghai Green was selected in the 1970s by the Shanghai Municipal Agricultural Science Research Institute for disease resistance and quick, uniform growth, and it bolts fast once days lengthen and warm, so time spring sowings to finish before the heat sets in.

directions: Broadcast or row-sow seed thinly and thin to final spacing once seedlings have two true leaves, since crowding pushes this compact type to bolt prematurely. Shanghai Green forms a tight, vase-shaped rosette of dark jade, spoon-shaped leaves on pale green, celery-like petioles, and its dwarf habit makes it one of the most reliable baby bok choy types for close spacing and container growing. Keep soil evenly moist and feed lightly, since even brief drought or a nutrient check can trigger bolting in warm weather. Harvest whole heads at 5-6 inches tall for the classic baby size, or let plants grow on another week or two for slightly larger heads with the same tender, mild flavor.

common_name: Numane Pickling Melon (Oshiro Uri Japanese Pickling Melon)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after soil has warmed well past last frost; Numane is a heat-loving traditional Japanese pickling melon and will sulk or rot in cold, wet soil.

directions: Give vines a trellis or ample ground space, since Numane produces long, vigorous runners that can sprawl 8-10 feet if left unsupported. This oshiro uri type bears pale green, smooth-skinned fruit up to a foot long that resembles an overgrown cucumber but has crisp, nearly white flesh with almost no sweetness, the traditional starting point for Japanese narazuke and shiozuke pickles. Harvest fruit while still firm and immature for pickling, or let a few size up and use the mature flesh in stir-fries, since overripe melons turn soft and seedy. Pick regularly to keep the vine productive through the heat of summer.

planting.note: Direct sow in deeply worked soil in late summer for a fall harvest, or early spring once soil is workable; Aokubi is the standard F1 daikon grown across most of Japan and tolerates a range of conditions better than many heirloom strains.

directions: Direct sow a half inch deep in loose, stone-free soil and thin early to prevent forked roots. Aokubi gets its name, meaning 'green neck,' from the shoulder of the root that pushes up out of the soil and turns light green where sunlight hits it, while the buried lower two-thirds stays pure white; this exposed shoulder also makes the root easy to grip and pull. Roots size up quickly and hold well in the ground without turning pithy, with a sweet flavor and crisp texture suited to grating, simmering, and fresh salads. Mulch around the shoulders if you want a fully white root for a more traditional presentation.

planting.note: Direct sow in late summer in deeply worked soil for a long, slow fall-to-winter finish; Nerima needs more time than quick commercial daikon types to develop its signature long, tapering root.

directions: Sow directly into deeply tilled, stone-free soil since this long heirloom root forks or distorts in compacted or shallow beds. Named for the Tokyo district where it was developed generations ago, Nerima produces a slender, tapering, mostly below-ground root historically prized above all other daikon for making takuan, the crunchy yellow pickled radish served throughout Japan. Roots hold their dense, fibrous texture well through curing and fermentation, which is exactly the quality that made this variety the traditional choice for pickling rather than fresh eating. Harvest in late fall once roots reach full size and before hard freezes, and allow a few days of post-harvest withering if preparing for traditional sun-dried pickling.

common_name: Mara Bitter Gourd (Mild Hybrid Bitter Melon)

planting.note: Start indoors 3-4 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay warm; Mara is a vigorous hybrid that wants consistent heat (80-90F) to germinate reliably and grow well.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and provide a sturdy trellis, since vines can climb 10-15 feet in a single warm season. Mara is a hybrid bitter gourd bred to be noticeably milder than typical Indian bitter melon types, producing large, cylindrical, shiny green fruit up to 11 inches long and about a pound each, with a flavor that stays lightly bitter raw but mellows further with cooking. Harvest while the skin is still glossy and firm, before fruit begins to yellow or soften, for the best balance of crunch and mild flavor. Pick promptly and often, since mature fruit left on the vine turns orange, splits open, and signals the plant to slow new fruit set.

common_name: Akasanjaku Yard Long Bean (Red-Seeded Japanese Asparagus Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed well past last frost danger; Akasanjaku thrives in sustained summer heat and is slower to establish in cool soil than common snap beans.

directions: Sow directly at the base of a tall trellis or pole support, since vines regularly climb 8-12 feet in warm weather. Akasanjaku takes its name from its distinctive brick-red dried seeds, though the harvested pods themselves are a pencil-thin, stringless light green that reach 12-16 inches long and stay tender well past the size where Western pole beans would toughen. This heat-loving heirloom is a traditional favorite for Sichuan-style dry-fried beans, where the pods are cooked hot and fast until blistered. Pick pods every two to three days once vines start bearing to encourage continuous production through the hottest part of summer, since any mature, seed-filled pods left on the vine slow new flowering.
